messages.author: f60c1eea3e0aa370
messages.subject: Adding random effects to make.lincombs
parts:
Hi
I have a model like
n <- 5380
ID <- seq(1:n)

r1 <- inla(respvar ~ -1 + Intercept + expvar1 + expvar2 + expvar3 + f(ID, model = 'iid') + f(w, model = open_spde,
data = inla.stack.data(mystack),
control.compute = control.compute = list(dic = T, waic = T, cpo = T),
control.predictor = list(compute = T, A = inla.stack.A(mystack))

Now I want to evaluate the effect of the fixed effects and the random effects individually on the values predicted by the model. In traditional mixed effects models you'd call this the marginal and conditional R-squared, i.e. how much does the random effects and the fixed effects contribute to the model respectively. I believe (and have tried without luck) that this maybe can be achieved with linear combinations, but could someone please direct me in a direction? Ideally with some example code, that shows how to enter the random effects into make.lincombs if that is the way to go. Maybe there is no good solution to this problem?

messages.author: 14f33f5ab5b4a1db
messages.subject: Re: Adding random effects to make.lincombs
parts: You can view distribution information for the fixed and random effects via r1$summary.fixed and r1$summary.random to see how much each term contributed to a given observation. Does this sound like what you want?

The ...eval function is a little special, as it assign simulated values
to each component in the model automatically. like if

y ~ x + f(z, model="...")

then

inla.posterior.sample.eval(
function() {
## here 'x' will be the regression coefficient

## while 'z' will be the vector defined by f(z, ..)

## so if we want the Predictor (which is also
## an automatic variable) then we need to
## pass the covariates 'x', but now 'x' means
## the regression coefficent, so that require
## a small fix...
})


like

fun = function (x.cov) { return (Intercept + x * xx.cov + z) }

and then pass x.cov in the args

inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, samples, x.cox=data$x)

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Adding random effects to make.lincombs
parts:
On Wed, 2022-08-24 at 04:07 -0700, Jesper Erenskjold Moeslund wrote:
> Thanks a lot for this elaboration. Three questions arise.
> 1: I still do not understand the v.index in your example. Where does
> the function get this index from when you call v.index? Is ".index"
> some built-in function that does something I apparently cannot read
> anywhere I have searched? And shouldn't it be v.idx.index in any case?
> The code runs, so probably not, I just don't understand why.
>

it is just a 'naming' thing.

f(i)

this can be interpreted as effect 'f' indexed by 'i', so

f[i]

in vector/R notation, so that

y ~ 1 + x + f(i)

means

Predictor = Intercept + beta.x * x + f[i]


in the 'eval' function, then 'beta.x' is named 'x' (as usual in lm/glm),
whereas 'f' is named 'x', then we need

Predictor = Intercept + x * x.covariate + i[i.index]

where 'x.covariate' is the 'x-covariate', and 'i.index' is 'i' as above


so

fun = function(x.covariate, i.index) 
return (Intercept + x * x.covariate + i[i.index])

with

...eval(..., x.covariate=x, i.index=i)

where 'x' and 'i' is in the formula above.

> 2: Is it correct that in the function, given the example above, you
> could write either:
>        function () { return (Intercept + Predictor + z) }
> or
>        function (xcov1, xcov2,...) { return (Intercept + x1 * xcov1 +
> x2 * xcov2 ... + z)}
> or is this totally misunderstood?

The 'Predictor' is the linear predictor, hence the sum of all terms in
the formula, so with

y ~ 1 + x + f(i)

the Predictor = Intercept + beta.x * x + f[i]

>
> 3: Why couldn't the function in the first and really nice example not
> be:
> function () { return c(Intercept + Predictor, Intercept + Predictor -
> v.idx) }
> >

'v.idx' is likely of a different length then 'Predictor' and/or the
index ordering is not the same, hence you need to index that one to get
it right.

Note that 'Intercept' is part of 'Predictor' hence not needed.

please try out with some small simple examples to make sure you get
understand it correct.



there should be a vignette about this, if anyone... please let me know


--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

>       }
> and then you used that function in ...eval:

> GIVEN HERE), samples)
> But as I have tried to highlight above, you do not pass any arguments
> to the function. How does the function "know" what v.index is? It is
> defined to require an argument, but no arguments are given?

aah, sure, you have to pass v.index=data$v.idx, or where its stored in
...eval().

>
> 2: Is it correct that I should use the APredictor in my case (maybe
> has to do with the spatial random effect, but I can't find their
> differences described anywhere)? It seems like the Predictor has some
> very different values from what I'd expect and nothing close to my
> original observed values whereas the APredictor gives me values like I
> would expect.

yes, for the spde model using 'stack' then 'APredictor' is defined as

APredictor = pA %*% Predictor

where 'pA' the mapping matrix, in the argument

control.predictor=list(A=..)

and this is

If this is used, the 'pA' should be available in the function to be
evaluated as you need it. which I see it is currently not. that needs to
be fixed.

meanwhile, you can pass

...eval(...., pA = result$misc$configs$pA)

and then use

no.random = pA %*% ( Predictor - v.idx[v.index])

please check with simple example that this is correct.




--
